extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, and patent applicants (prosecutors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and case examples for assessing patentability and inventive step (obviousness), including how to compare claims to prior art, determine differences, evaluate common general technical knowledge, and assess technical effects and motivations to combine references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical character / patentable subject matter (Article 2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A solution processed by a computer that uses technical data (e.g., text data or semantic information) and solves a technical problem by technical means to obtain corresponding technical effects constitutes a technical solution under Article 2.2 and thus is eligible as an 'invention'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claimed method concretely implements information processing via cooperation of software and hardware resources; verify the data processed are technical in nature and that the invention solves a technical problem using technical means and produces technical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step / Obviousness assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the invention involves an inventive step by comparing the claimed invention with cited prior art and common general technical knowledge to see if a person skilled in the art could easily derive the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify distinguishing features, assess whether substitution/combination with known techniques would be obvious, consider whether expected effects are predictable, and look for obstructive factors; conclude 'involves an inventive step' when differences are non-obvious and produce significant unexpected technical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify differences between claim and cited art
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step is to identify the point(s) of difference (distinguishing features) between the claimed invention and the cited document(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly list differing claim elements (e.g., neural network vs regression model; inclusion of certain input variables); base subsequent assessment on these identified differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of whether differences are obvious to a person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying differences, assess whether a person skilled in the art could have easily derived the distinguishing features by applying common knowledge or by combining cited documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider known practices in the technical field, whether the substitution/combination would be a mere workshop modification or routine design choice, and whether any obstructive factors exist that would prevent the skilled person from making the change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common general technical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a technical fact (e.g., that temperature affects inflow/meltwater or that selecting correlated inputs improves ML accuracy) was common general technical knowledge at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a matter is common general technical knowledge, adding or using it is more likely to be considered obvious; use expert knowledge of the field to decide whether the fact was commonly known at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance/unexpectedness of technical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the technical effect produced by the distinguishing feature is significant and not predictable by a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the effect (e.g., markedly improved estimation accuracy due to inclusion of a novel input) is a significant effect that a skilled person could not expect, this supports inventive step; document why the effect is non-obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine prior art references
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether there was a motivation for a person skilled in the art to combine teachings of multiple cited documents to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider factors such as (1) relation of technical fields, (2) similarity of the problem to be solved, and (3) similarity of the functions/results of the cited disclosures; if the combination is motivated and predictable, it supports obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of obstructive factors or disincentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether any disincentive or technical difficulty would have deterred a skilled person from making the proposed modification or combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of obstructive factors makes derivation from prior art more plausible; presence of non-trivial obstacles supports non-obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of algorithmic features interacting with technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether algorithmic (e.g., neural network) and technical (hardware/data) features functionally support each other and have an interaction relationship that yields a technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the algorithmic aspects produce or enhance a concrete technical effect via interaction with technical features, that interaction strengthens technical character and may support inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of the technical problem actually solved
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify the technical problem that the invention actually solves as a basis for inventive-step analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the problem in technical terms (e.g., improving inference accuracy in semantic search) and use it to evaluate whether prior art would have motivated the claimed solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether claimed additions are mere design variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide if the distinguishing features amount to routine design variation or choice that a skilled person would make without inventive ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label as obvious when the change is a predictable design selection (e.g., adding known sensor variables) rather than a non-routine technical advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of domain-specific common practices (machine learning inputs)
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing inventions involving machine learning, consider the well-known practice of adopting input variables likely correlated with outputs to enhance reliability and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where this is common practice, adding plausible correlated inputs (e.g., temperature) may be considered an obvious optimization unless an unexpected technical effect is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of cited documents plus common knowledge to show obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention may be considered obvious if the combination of prior documents and common general technical knowledge would lead a skilled person to the claimed solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly demonstrate how each element of the claim is disclosed or suggested by the combination; show that no obstructive factor exists and that the expected effect would have been foreseen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation by software/hardware cooperation as evidence of technical subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing that a claimed method establishes a mathematical model and is implemented concretely by cooperating software and hardware supports finding that it is a technical invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate concrete implementation details (software using hardware resources) rather than mere abstract algorithms to support patentable technical character.
